sn12.1:1.1: For an overview of this topic, see my Introduction to the Saṁyutta Nikāya.
sn12.1:1.3: In a shift from the previous book, there is no interaction or dialogue; the teaching is a direct address by the Buddha.
sn12.1:2.1: Most of these terms can be identified as pre-Buddhist. The Buddha redefined them to his own purpose, which we find in the next discourse. Here I give the pre-Buddhist usage so we can understand what the Buddha was responding to.
sn12.1:2.2: “Knowledge” (_veda_) was that of the immortal gods, so knowledge itself is immortal, while ignorance, being perishable, trapping the fool in suffering for life after life. Knowledge and ignorance are part of the mortal condition (Atharva Veda 11.8.23). “A man crosses death through ignorance and attains immortality through knowledge” (Īśa Upaniṣad 11; cf. Paiṅgala Upaniṣad 2.11, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.1, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9).
sn12.1:2.4: One who is dying becomes mere consciousness savijñano bhavati | saṃjānam evānvavakrāmati | taṃ vidyākarmaṇī samanvārabhete pūrvaprajñā ca || Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2
sn12.1:2.14: There is no corresponding “dependent cessation”. The ending of dependent origination is Nibbana, extinguishment.
